advances: This excludes the entire affine-dimension-two source case of the necessary inner-body problem. In conjunction with the actual-section reduction in accepted fact 3472b436c1c4f05f, any remaining forty-two-point width-two example must have a three-dimensional source hull. No exclusion of that three-dimensional case is asserted.
author: research-agent
external_sources:
M. Blanco, C. Haase, J. Hofmann, and F. Santos, *The finiteness threshold width of lattice polytopes*, arXiv:1607.00798v3, 4 January 2021, Theorem 5.2 and Lemma 5.3, printed pages 16–17: [primary paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1607.00798v3).

The exact classification used is: up to affine lattice isomorphism, the hollow three-dimensional lattice polytopes of width greater than two are precisely \(M_3,M_5,M_6,M_9,M_{10}\), all of width three. The first three are the displayed tetrahedra; the other two have five and six vertices. Lemma 5.3 classifies the polytopes themselves, and its proof checks all single-vertex deletions from the maximal representatives. Its hypotheses apply to a prospective hollow \(K\) by the width argument above. The three tetrahedral possibilities were excluded by the explicit census and reflection checks in the proof.
proof:
We first prove the assertion about an arbitrary twenty-point tetrahedron \(K\), independently of the source \(Q\). Accepted fact 768d9712b73c4ab7 gives \(|B|\le3\cdot2^\ell-v_B\) for a full-dimensional lattice-convex support in its intrinsic rank-\(\ell\) lattice, where \(v_B\) is its number of vertices. To apply this to a lower-dimensional section, translate one lattice point to zero and choose a basis of the lattice in its linear span. Every reflected displacement in that lattice is an ambient integer displacement, so the reflection bound is inherited. Thus the maximum sizes in ranks zero, one, and two are respectively \(1,4,9\).

The lattice width of \(K\) is at least three. A primitive integer functional of width one would give only two nonempty integer sections, with at most nine points each. At width two the middle section has at most nine points. If the endpoint faces have dimensions \(\delta_0,\delta_2\), their disjoint vertex sets use at least \(\delta_0+\delta_2+2\) of the tetrahedron's four vertices. Hence \(\delta_0+\delta_2\le2\). The two endpoint sections together have at most ten points, attained among these bounds only by the dimension pair \((2,0)\) or \((0,2)\); the pair \((1,1)\) permits only eight. Width two therefore permits at most nineteen points, also a contradiction.

We use the precise hollow-polytope classification stated in EXTERNAL SOURCES below. A hollow lattice tetrahedron of width greater than two must be affine-unimodularly equivalent to one of

\[
\begin{aligned}
M_3&=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(3,0,0),(0,3,0),(0,0,3)\},\\
M_5&=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(2,5,0),(3,0,5)\},\\
M_6&=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(3,0,0),(1,3,0),(2,0,3)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

In \(M_3\), the center \((1,1,0)\) has the three distinct unordered endpoint pairs
\((0,1,0),(2,1,0)\),
\((1,0,0),(1,2,0)\), and
\((0,2,0),(2,0,0)\).
All six endpoints belong to \(M_3\), so its reflection count there is at least seven.

For \(M_5\), barycentric coordinates give exactly the membership inequalities \(y,z\ge0\) and \(2y+3z\le5x\le5+y+2z\). They imply \(y+z\le5\). For \(M_6\), the inequalities are \(y,z\ge0\), \(y+2z\le3x\), and \(3x+2y+z\le9\), implying \(y+z\le3\). The following complete integer censuses follow by taking the ceiling of each lower bound on \(x\) and the floor of each upper bound. Each entry lists all pairs \((x,y)\) at the indicated height.

~~~text
z    M5                                    M6
0    (0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(1,2),(2,5)         (0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(1,2),
                                           (1,3),(2,0),(2,1),(3,0)
1    (1,0),(1,1),(2,3)                     (1,0),(1,1),(2,0),(2,1)
2    (2,1),(2,2)                           (2,0)
3    (2,0)                                 (2,0)
4    none                                  no possible height
5    (3,0)                                 no possible height
~~~

Thus \(M_5\) and \(M_6\) have respectively twelve and fourteen lattice points. The classification applies to \(K\) because it is full-dimensional, integral, and was proved to have width greater than two. Its other two representatives have five and six vertices, so cannot be equivalent to a tetrahedron. All possible hollow cases have now been excluded. Consequently \(K\) has at least one interior lattice point.

Let \(J\ge1\) and \(B_\partial\) be the numbers of interior and boundary lattice points of \(K\), so \(B_\partial+J=20\). Triangulate its boundary using every boundary lattice point as a vertex. A triangulated sphere with \(B_\partial\) vertices has \(2B_\partial-4\) triangles, by Euler's formula and the fact that each edge belongs to two triangles. Cone this triangulation from one interior lattice point. This yields \(2B_\partial-4\) lattice tetrahedra. Insert each of the other \(J-1\) interior points by stellar subdivision. Each insertion increases the number of tetrahedra by at least three: a tetrahedron splits into four; an internal triangular face replaces two tetrahedra by six; and an internal edge has at least three incident tetrahedra, each of which splits into two. The last assertion follows because the incident dihedral angles, each strictly less than \(\pi\), sum to \(2\pi\). Every resulting tetrahedron has positive integer normalized volume. Therefore

\[
D\ge2B_\partial-4+3(J-1)
=2\cdot20+J-7
=33+J\ge34.
\]

We now retain the full source geometry. Write \(M=\mathbb Z^3\), \(s=u/2\), \(L=M+\mathbb Zs\), and \(E=Q/2\). Since \(u\) is primitive, it is not in \(2M\). Thus \(M\) has index two in \(L\), \(L\setminus M=s+M\), and \(2L=\Lambda'\). In particular,

\[
E\cap L=\{a,b,c-s,d-s\},\qquad
\mathcal R=E+[0,s],\qquad
K=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((E\cap M)\cup((E\cap(s+M))+s)\bigr).
\]

These are exact identities. The four points of \(E\cap L\) consist of two in each coset of \(M\), and \(K\subseteq\mathcal R\). Let \(\chi:L\to\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\) be the quotient character with kernel \(M\); hence \(\chi(s)=1\). Also \(s\) is primitive in \(L\): if \(s=t\ell\) with an integer \(t>1\) and \(\ell\in L\), then \(u=t(2\ell)\) with \(2\ell\in M\), contradicting primitivity of \(u\).

Two normalization operations will be used explicitly. Translation of \(E\) by a vector of \(M\) translates \(K\) and \(\mathcal R\) by that same vector and \(Q\) by twice that vector. We may also interchange the two coset roles: for \(v\in E\cap(s+M)\), replace \(E,s\) by \(E-v,-s\). The corresponding middle tetrahedron and prism become \(K-v-s\) and \(\mathcal R-v-s\), while the source becomes \(Q-2v\). Here \(v+s\in M\) and \(2v\in2L\subset M\). Hence all lattice counts, reflection bounds, and the relevant containment are preserved. These operations let us choose a convenient origin and, when necessary, reverse which of the four source points are in the first coset.

Translate a source point in \(M\) to the origin. The plane of \(E\) then has the rank-two lattice \(G=L\cap\operatorname{lin}(E)\). It is saturated in \(L\), so a basis of \(G\) extends to a basis of \(L\). The lattice-polygon area formula proved in accepted fact 3472b436c1c4f05f applies in \(G\): a polygon with \(N\) lattice points and \(b_\partial\) boundary lattice points has normalized area \(2N-b_\partial-2\). Since \(E\) has exactly four \(G\)-points and dimension two, it has either four vertices, or three vertices with its fourth point on the boundary or in the interior. We check all three cases.

If \(E\) has four vertices, it is an empty lattice parallelogram of normalized area two. Here is the needed classification directly. Triangulate it along a diagonal. The two triangles are empty and therefore have normalized area one, as proved in 3472b436c1c4f05f. Send three consecutive vertices to \(0,e_1,e_2\). The other vertex has coordinates \((-1,t)\): it is on the opposite side of the diagonal \([0,e_2]\) from \(e_1\), and its triangle with that diagonal has determinant one. Strict convexity at \(0\) and at \(e_2\) gives respectively \(t>0\) and \(t<2\), so \(t=1\). Thus we can write the four vertices as \(0,v,w,v+w\), with \(v,w\) a basis of \(G\).

If exactly one of \(\chi(v),\chi(w)\) is one, the two points of each coset are adjacent vertices. Shifting the two points of the second coset by \(s\) then leaves a parallelogram, contradicting the full dimension of \(K\). If both values are one, the two first-coset points are \(0,v+w\). In this case \(Q=2E\) contains the four points \(0,2v,2w,2(v+w)\) of \(M\). Their two distinct opposite pairs have the common center \(v+w\in M\). Including the zero displacement gives \(r_{Q\cap M}(v+w)\ge5\), a contradiction. The remaining possibility, both character values zero, would put all four points in the same coset. The quadrilateral case is therefore impossible.

Suppose the fourth point of the triangular \(E\) is on its boundary. The area formula gives normalized area two. Its edge containing that point has lattice length two, and the height of the opposite vertex in a basis of \(G\) is one. The two endpoints of the doubled edge differ by twice a vector of \(G\), so have the same character. Use the coset interchange above, if needed, to put them in the first coset, then translate one of them to zero. Taking the primitive edge direction as the first basis vector and applying a shear gives the exact four-point set \(\{0,e_1,2e_1,e_2\}\), with triangle \(\operatorname{conv}\{0,2e_1,e_2\}\). Having two points in each coset now forces \(\chi(e_1)=\chi(e_2)=1\).

Extend this plane basis to \(e_1,e_2,e_3\) of \(L\). If necessary replace \(e_3\) by \(e_3+e_1\), so that \(\chi(e_3)=0\). In these coordinates \(M=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb Z^3:x+y\text{ is even}\}\). The coordinate map \((x,y,z)\mapsto((x+y)/2,y,z)\) is a lattice isomorphism from this \(M\) onto the standard integer lattice. If \(s=(s_1,s_2,h)\) in the \(L\)-basis, put \(\alpha=(s_1+s_2+1)/2\) and \(\beta=s_2\), both integers. In the resulting \(M\)-coordinates the exact pair is

\[
\begin{aligned}
K&=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(\alpha,\beta,h),(\alpha,\beta+1,h)\},\\
\mathcal R&=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(1/2,1,0)\}
 +[0,(\alpha-1/2,\beta,h)].
\end{aligned}
\]

Finally suppose the fourth point of \(E\) is interior. Its normalized area is three. Coning its boundary from that point gives three empty triangles, each of normalized area one. For the planar classification alone, place the interior point at zero and two consecutive vertices at \(e_1,e_2\). The determinant-one conditions for the other two triangles force the third vertex to be \(-e_1-e_2\). This triangle has lattice automorphisms inducing every permutation of its three vertices: each adjacent pair of their vectors is a lattice basis. Translating a vertex to zero and applying a lattice basis change gives the equivalent four-point set \(\{0,e_1,(2,3),(1,1)\}\), with \((1,1)\) interior. For example, after translating \(-e_1-e_2\) to zero, the linear map \((x,y)\mapsto(y,-x+2y)\) sends the other vertices to \((1,0),(2,3)\) and the interior point to \((1,1)\).

To normalize the actual pair while retaining its lattice \(M\), first use the coset interchange, if needed, to put the interior point in the second coset. Choose a first-coset vertex as the origin. The vertex permutations just established let us arrange the normal form with the two first-coset vertices at \(0,(2,3)\), and the two second-coset points at \(e_1,(1,1)\). The translation used here is therefore by a vector of \(M\). The character in this basis is \(\chi(x,y)=x\pmod2\). Extend to a basis of \(L\) with \(\chi(e_3)=0\), as before. Now \(M\) consists of the integer coordinates with even \(x\), and \((x,y,z)\mapsto(x/2,y-3x/2,z)\) is a lattice isomorphism from \(M\) onto \(\mathbb Z^3\). Writing \(s=(s_1,s_2,h)\), set \(\alpha=(s_1+1)/2\) and \(\beta=s_2-3\alpha\). The exact pair becomes

\[
\begin{aligned}
K&=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(\alpha,\beta,h),(\alpha,\beta+1,h)\},\\
\mathcal R&=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(1/2,-3/2,0)\}
 +[0,(\alpha-1/2,\beta+3/2,h)].
\end{aligned}
\]

All these coordinate changes are lattice isomorphisms of the original \(M\), after the indicated changes of its basis; the coset interchange translates \(K\) and \(\mathcal R\) by an integer vector. We retain their names in the new coordinates. Thus their original integer counts and the normalized volume of \(K\) are unchanged. The two triangular cases above are exact descriptions of \(\mathcal R\), not supersets used to estimate it. Full dimension forces \(h\ne0\). Reverse the third coordinate if necessary to assume \(h>0\). The displayed vertex matrix of \(K\) has determinant of absolute value \(h\), so \(D=h\).

It remains to count integer points of these two actual prisms. We prove, for every pair of integers \(\alpha,\beta\) and every positive integer \(h\), that either displayed prism has at least \(\lfloor h/2\rfloor+4\) integer points. Every integer point has height \(j\in\{0,\ldots,h\}\). At height zero either base triangle has exactly the two points \((0,0),(1,0)\). At height \(h\), either translated triangle has exactly the two points \((\alpha,\beta),(\alpha,\beta+1)\). This gives four endpoint points.

For an intermediate height \(j\), put \(t=j/h\). In both cases the vertical symmetry axis of the triangular section has abscissa \(X_j=\alpha t+(1-t)/2\). Choose an integer \(x_j\) nearest to \(X_j\), and put \(d_j=|x_j-X_j|\in[0,1/2]\). Ties may be resolved arbitrarily. The vertical interval of the section at this integer abscissa is, respectively,

\[
J_j=
\begin{cases}
[\beta t,\ \beta t+1-2d_j],&\text{in the boundary-point triangular case},\\
[(\beta+3/2)t-3/2+3d_j,\ (\beta+3/2)t],&\text{in the interior-point triangular case}.
\end{cases}
\]

Each integer in \(J_j\) supplies an integer point \((x_j,y,j)\) of the actual prism. The identity \(X_j+X_{h-j}=\alpha+1/2\) implies \(d_j+d_{h-j}=1/2\): the distances of two real numbers whose sum is an integer plus one-half to the nearest integers sum to one-half.

Consider first a pair of distinct heights \(j,h-j\), with \(1\le j<h/2\). In the boundary-point case, put \(Y=\beta t\). Reflect the interval \(J_{h-j}\) by the integer-preserving map \(y\mapsto\beta-y\). The resulting interval is \([Y-(1-2d_{h-j}),Y]\), whereas \(J_j=[Y,Y+1-2d_j]\). Their union is a closed interval of length one. It contains an integer, and therefore the two distinct height sections contribute at least one integer point between them.

In the interior-point case put \(Y=(\beta+3/2)t\). The same integer-preserving reflection sends \(J_{h-j}\) to \([Y-3/2,Y-3d_{h-j}]\). Its right endpoint is \(Y-3/2+3d_j\), exactly the left endpoint of \(J_j\). Their union is the closed interval \([Y-3/2,Y]\) of length three-halves, again containing an integer. The two height sections therefore contribute at least one integer point in this case as well.

If \(h\) is even, the remaining middle height \(j=h/2\) has \(X_j=\alpha/2+1/4\), so \(d_j=1/4\). Its selected vertical interval is \([\beta/2,\beta/2+1/2]\) in the first case and \([\beta/2,\beta/2+3/4]\) in the second. Each contains an integer, whether \(\beta\) is even or odd. We have accounted for every intermediate height, in pairs and, when necessary, this singleton. Together with the four endpoint points this proves

\[
|\mathcal R\cap\mathbb Z^3|
\ge4+\left\lfloor\frac h2\right\rfloor
=4+\left\lfloor\frac D2\right\rfloor
\ge21,
\]

where the last inequality uses the independently proved \(D\ge34\). Since \(K\subseteq\mathcal R\) and \(K\) has exactly twenty integer points, at least one of these integer points lies outside \(K\). This proves the rank-two assertion without any restriction on a source determinant, a direction search, or an unexamined integer height.
statement:
Use the oriented, zero-inclusive reflection convention of accepted fact 768d9712b73c4ab7: for a finite lattice-convex set \(B\subseteq\mathbb Z^3\) and every \(j\in\mathbb Z^3\), let \(r_B(j)=|\{v\in\mathbb Z^3:j+v,j-v\in B\}|\). The letter \(K\) denotes the middle tetrahedron, as in accepted fact 3472b436c1c4f05f; it is not the curvature quantity from other parts of the project.

Let \(K=\operatorname{conv}\{a,b,c,d\}\subset\mathbb R^3\) be a full-dimensional lattice tetrahedron with \(|K\cap\mathbb Z^3|=20\) and \(\max_j r_{K\cap\mathbb Z^3}(j)\le3\). Let \(u\in\mathbb Z^3\) be primitive, and set \(Q=\operatorname{conv}\{2a,2b,2c-u,2d-u\}\) and \(\Lambda'=2\mathbb Z^3+\mathbb Zu\). Suppose that \(Q\) has affine dimension two, that its intersection with \(\Lambda'\) consists of exactly those four displayed distinct points, and that \(\max_j r_{Q\cap\mathbb Z^3}(j)\le3\).

Then \(\mathcal R=(Q+[0,u])/2\) has at least twenty-one integer points. In particular, \(\mathcal R\) contains an integer point outside \(K\).

The proof also establishes the structural input it uses: every twenty-point lattice tetrahedron with reflection maximum at most three has an interior lattice point and has normalized volume at least thirty-four. Normalized volume here is \(D=|\det(b-a,c-a,d-a)|\), or six times ordinary volume in \(\mathbb Z^3\).
